front: What are the three classes of lever?
back: First-class lever = Effort–Fulcrum–Resistance; Second-class lever = Fulcrum–Resistance–Effort; Third-class lever = Fulcrum–Effort–Resistance.

front: What are examples of first-class levers in the body?
back: Flexion and extension of the head and neck; extension of the elbow using the triceps.

front: What is an example of a second-class lever in the body?
back: Plantar flexion at the ankle, such as pushing up onto the toes when jumping for a header.

front: What are examples of third-class levers in the body?
back: Most levers in the body are third class; examples include flexion at the elbow using the biceps and flexion at the hip and knee.

front: What are two benefits of lever systems?
back: They can allow a large resistance to be moved with a relatively small effort, or increase the speed and range of movement at the end of a lever.

front: What happens when the fulcrum is closer to the resistance in a first-class lever?
back: The effort arm becomes longer than the resistance arm, creating a mechanical advantage and allowing a larger resistance to be moved with less effort.

front: What happens when the fulcrum is closer to the effort in a first-class lever?
back: The resistance arm becomes longer, creating a mechanical disadvantage but allowing greater speed and range of movement at the resistance end.

front: Why is the position of the fulcrum important in a lever system?
back: It affects the relative lengths of the effort and resistance arms, influencing mechanical advantage, force, speed and range of movement.

front: What is an advantage of a second-class lever?
back: It has a mechanical advantage, allowing a large resistance to be moved with a relatively small effort.

front: What is a disadvantage of a second-class lever?
back: It produces less speed and range of movement at the resistance end compared with a third-class lever.

front: What is an advantage of first- and third-class levers?
back: They can provide a large range of movement and high speed at the end of the lever when operating with a mechanical disadvantage.

front: What is a disadvantage of first- and third-class levers?
back: When operating with a mechanical disadvantage, a relatively large effort is required to move the resistance.

front: What is mechanical advantage and what is its formula?
back: Mechanical advantage occurs when the effort arm is longer than the resistance arm, allowing a relatively small effort to move a larger resistance; Mechanical advantage = Effort arm ÷ Resistance arm.

front: What are the features of a mechanical advantage?
back: A relatively small effort can move a larger resistance; the effort arm is longer than the resistance arm; second-class levers always have a mechanical advantage.
A mechanical disadvantage occurs when the resistance arm is longer than the effort arm, meaning a greater effort is required to move the resistance.

front: What are the features of a mechanical disadvantage?
back: Third-class levers always have a mechanical disadvantage; they can increase the speed and range of movement at the end of the lever.
